clippings.caption: Colonel Murrell, editor of the New Jersey Trumpet, was then introduced as the speaker of the evening.
clippings.alt: Asbury Park Press front page from July 22, 1893, headlined 'Final settlement,' reporting on a mass meeting where Colonel Murrell of the New Jersey Trumpet spoke.

clippings.caption: ECHO MOVES TO RED BANK. The Echo edited and published in the interest of the colored race in Long Branch by W. E. Rock for the past five years, has moved to Red Bank, where Editor Rock has purchased a home.
clippings.alt: Asbury Park Press clipping from March 5, 1909, headlined 'Echo moves to Red Bank,' reporting the Echo newspaper's relocation from Long Branch.

clippings.caption: Photo cutline: Melvin B. Johnson, former editor and publisher of weekly newspapers at Montclair and Newark.
clippings.alt: Asbury Park Press clipping from November 6, 1949, with a photo of Melvin B. Johnson, former editor and publisher of weekly newspapers in Montclair and Newark.

clippings.caption: Asbury Park Press Lakewood column: a book to be published in the July issue of Bronze Thrills.
clippings.alt: Asbury Park Press 'Lakewood Area' column from May 20, 1960, mentioning a book to be published in the July issue of Bronze Thrills.

clippings.caption: AP obit: Harry B. Webber, city editor of the New Jersey Herald News, then editor and publisher of After Hours, a Newark magazine, in the 1940s.
clippings.alt: Courier-News obituary from June 24, 1991, headlined 'Harry B. Webber, 90, former newspaper editor,' who edited and published After Hours magazine in Newark.

clippings.caption: Courier-Post: Ironsides Echo, monthly student paper of the Bordentown Manual Training School, won second place in the Columbia Scholastic Press contest. Student editor Leon Snead.
clippings.alt: Courier-Post clipping from March 22, 1932, headlined 'Training school wins praise for newspaper,' about the Ironsides Echo winning a Columbia scholastic press award.

clippings.caption: Courier-Post: CCC Company 1275 at Erlton started a journalism class and turns out a paper, Camp Cooper, regularly. Educational advisor A. W. Reed.
clippings.alt: Courier-Post clipping from January 6, 1936, headlined 'School, dances and athletics build character in C.C.C. camp,' describing the Camp Cooper newspaper at Erlton.

clippings.caption: The New Jersey Afro-American — published in Newark — was one of a chain of Black-owned and edited papers... the New Jersey edition no longer exists.
clippings.alt: Daily Record (Morristown) clipping from May 21, 2023, reproducing a 1947 New Jersey Afro-American front page headlined '1946: Year of great Negro resistance to hate groups.'

clippings.caption: Colored Newspaper Burned Out. The Echo, a weekly negro newspaper published at Long Branch, was burned out recently. The fire which is thought to be of incendiary origin damaged the machinery and press-room of the newspaper to the extent of several hundred dollars. The first issue of the paper was edited by Rock & Howard.
clippings.alt: Monmouth Democrat clipping from September 8, 1904, headlined 'Colored newspaper burned out,' reporting a fire at the Echo's Long Branch offices.

clippings.caption: Tom Brady on Alfred P. Smith: The Landscape, first as A.P. Smith's Paper, printed at East Allendale Road from May 1881 until July 1901.
clippings.alt: Ridgewood News page from November 26, 1987, headlined 'Newspaper of days ago remembered,' with a portrait of Alfred P. Smith, editor of The Landscape.

clippings.caption: Colonel Murrell, editor of the New Jersey Trumpet, later James A. Bradley entered and was greeted with applause. The meeting was called to discuss the signs which James A. Bradley had posted on the pavilions forbidding their occupancy to the colored race.
clippings.alt: Shore Press clipping from July 28, 1893, headlined 'Final settlement,' describing Colonel Murrell's remarks at the Asbury Park indignation meeting.

clippings.caption: Melvin B. Johnson named as former Negro newspaper publisher and editor, in the field until 1946.
clippings.alt: Star-Ledger clipping from January 19, 1949, naming Melvin B. Johnson as a former Negro newspaper publisher and editor, beside a photo of Frank Miller.

clippings.caption: Nancy R. Peck: Alfred P. Smith printed what was called the nation's smallest newspaper from an old house overlooking the Saddle River valley.
clippings.alt: Sunday News (Ridgewood) clipping from June 27, 1993, headlined 'Big, small issues filled tiny 1882 newspaper,' about Alfred P. Smith's Landscape.

clippings.caption: Second Look: Writer shaped civil-rights Landscape. Alfred P. Smith started A. P. Smith's Paper in 1881, then renamed it The Landscape.
clippings.alt: The Record (Hackensack) 'Second look' column from February 9, 1991, headlined 'Writer shaped civil-rights Landscape,' profiling publisher Alfred P. Smith.

clippings.caption: R. HENRI HERBERT'S ATTACK. He Asks His Colored Fellow-Citizens to Help Defeat Founder Bradley.

clippings.caption: R. HENRI HERBERT NOT LEFT. Appointed as a Consulting Member of the Republican State Committee.
